title: Envy, softened
hook: mudita's far enemy is envy; its near enemy is giddy excitement

segments.voice: Yesterday: mudita, gladness at someone else's good fortune. Your line: their joy is joy. A new week, and the two enemies at that room's door.

Envy may be the hardest feeling to own up to. People say they're angry, sad, tired, anxious. Fewer say, out loud, I'm envious of my sister. It shows up anyway: scrolling past a colleague's promotion, a neighbor's new kitchen, a friend's easy-looking marriage. It tightens something, and then comes a little story to make it hurt less: they got lucky, it won't last, it's not really that great.
screen: `THE FEELING FEW ADMIT.` → `THE PROMOTION, THE NEW KITCHEN.` → `A STORY TO MAKE IT HURT LESS.`

segments.voice: The Visuddhimagga's own name for mudita's far enemy is arati, aversion or discontent, the sour, fed-up feeling about someone else's good fortune. It says mudita's job is to be unenvious, so some modern teachers simply call the far enemy envy, the Pali issa. They're close cousins: envy is discontent with a target. It's the far enemy because it's the plain opposite of rejoicing. Where mudita says, how wonderful for you, envy says, why you and not me? The near enemy is subtler. The manual calls it joy based on the worldly life, a kind of excitement. Giddy excitement looks like mudita from the outside: exclamation points, big reactions. But it's often about me: the thrill of the party, of being close to someone's success, of the gossip about it. It's bubbly, it fades quickly, and sometimes it curdles into envy the next morning. Real mudita is steadier and quieter. It stays glad even when you're not in the photo. So how does envy soften? The manual's advice is the same gentle order as with every room. Start with someone easy to be glad for, and let the gladness grow strong. Then turn it, a little at a time, toward someone harder. And underneath sits a simple fact: someone else's happiness doesn't use up the world's supply. Their promotion isn't taken from your drawer. When that lands, even briefly, envy has less to hold on to, and what was a tight fist can open into joy.
screen: `FAR ENEMY: ARATI, AND ISSA, ENVY.` · `WHY YOU AND NOT ME?` · `NEAR ENEMY: GIDDY EXCITEMENT.` · `JOY ISN'T IN SHORT SUPPLY.` · then, large: `ENVY SOFTENS INTO JOY.`

segments.voice: Warm up with someone easy to be glad for, then gently bring to mind one person you envy a little, not the hardest one, and notice the tightening without scolding it. Picture their good fortune making their day better, just as your good days make yours better. Then offer one breath of the wish, may your good fortune last; if it's stiff, that's all right.
Envy. Mudita's far enemy, the plain opposite of rejoicing; its near enemy is giddy excitement that's really about me.
Your line: envy softens into joy. Slowly, from easy people to harder ones. Day two hundred thirty-nine, done.

howItsDone: Meditation teachers present envy and excited, self-centered joy as the far and near enemies of mudita, and guide students to rejoice first for easy people and then, gradually, for people they envy.

original.note: Pali issā: envy; the manual names mudita's far enemy arati (discontent), which some modern teachers call envy.

trapdoor: what you thought: envy is just wanting what others have.
what it means: discontent at someone else's good fortune, mudita's far enemy; its near enemy is excitement that's really about me.

what a scholar hears: Visuddhimagga IX names arati (aversion/boredom) as the far enemy and gehasita somanassa, worldly joy, as the near enemy; its function is being unenvious, so issa, envy, is what mudita removes.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga IX (mudita: near and far enemies, function)

notes: The outline's hook says mudita's far enemy is envy; the Visuddhimagga (IX.95, IX.100) names aversion/boredom (arati) as the far enemy, with 'being unenvious' as mudita's function. The script says this plainly and keeps the index wording as the modern teachers' reading.
Near enemy: 'joy based on the home life' (gehasita somanassa), rendered as giddy, self-centered excitement. Confirm the gloss.
Mudita's function as 'being unenvious' (Vsm IX.95): confirm the Pali wording before adding it.
